overview.title: Ghost Rider, decade by decade
overview.lede: Ghost Rider exists because of a rule change. The Comics Code was rewritten in 1971 to allow vampires, werewolves and demons back into American comics for the first time since 1954, and Marvel spent the next three years filling the gap — Tomb of Dracula, Werewolf by Night, Man-Thing, and a stunt motorcyclist who sold his soul. This shelf does not start there, because that run has never been collected in omnibus. It starts in 1990 with the man who replaced him, and the seven books on it disagree completely about whether the Ghost Rider is a curse, a weapon, an angel, a joke, or a haunting.

sections.h: The one that is not on this shelf
body: Marvel Spotlight #5, August 1972: Gary Friedrich, Roy Thomas and Mike Ploog put a stunt rider named Johnny Blaze in front of Satan to buy his dying mentor another year, and the deal costs him a head. Seven issues of Spotlight, then eighty-one issues of his own title through to 1983.

Ploog had been Will Eisner's assistant, and it shows on every page: loose brushed contour, faces built out of a few decisive strokes, and a willingness to let a panel be mostly black. It is a horror comic drawn by someone trained on The Spirit, and it looks nothing like the Marvel house style around it.

The strangest thing in the run is real and worth knowing: in 1974 the book had Jesus Christ turn up and save Johnny Blaze, in a story Marvel then had redrawn and retconned into a Satanic illusion after the fact. Nothing else in this period is quite that unguarded.

None of it has an omnibus. Eleven years, the whole Ploog era, and the entirety of Johnny Blaze's first life are Epic Collections and Masterworks only, which is why this shelf opens eighteen years later.

fig.cap: Left: Marvel Spotlight #5, 1972 — Ploog. Right: the 1973 ongoing. Neither is on this shelf.

makers.b: Look at the edges. Ploog does not outline a figure in a clean even line the way the rest of 1972 Marvel does — he brushes it, so the contour thickens and vanishes and a shoulder can dissolve into the dark behind it. That is Eisner's habit, and it is why a Ploog horror page reads as atmosphere rather than as costume.

sections.h: Danny Ketch, and the best-selling book in the building
body: Marvel relaunched the title in May 1990 with a new man in the head: Danny Ketch, a teenager who finds a wrecked motorcycle in a Cypress Hills scrapyard, touches its gas cap and burns. Howard Mackie wrote it for the whole decade.

The single decision that made it work is that the Rider is not Danny. It does the talking, it decides who is guilty, it does not take instruction, and Danny spends years frightened of it. The Penance Stare arrives here: look into its eyes and you feel every hurt you have ever caused, at once. That is a horror-comic punishment rather than a punch, and it is the thing everybody remembers.

Javier Saltares laid the book out and Mark Texeira came in over him from #6, first inking and then drawing it outright, and the look he arrived at — scratched, feathered, more black on the page than not — became the visual grammar of the whole early 90s. The title was one of the best-selling comics Marvel published in those years.
It was also the right character at the right commercial moment: leather, a chain, a bike, a skull. Everything the speculator boom wanted.

fig.cap: Left: #1, 1990. Right: #15 — Texeira, and almost the entire cover is black.

makers.b: Count how much of a Texeira page is solid black. He builds a figure by carving light out of the dark rather than by drawing a line and filling it, and the flames are left as bare paper. On a character who is literally a fire in a leather jacket that is not a style choice, it is the correct engineering.
Watch who is speaking in a Ghost Rider scene. Mackie almost never lets Danny and the Rider agree, and a lot of the run's tension is one character being a passenger in his own book.

sections.h: The Midnight Sons, and a horror line built on one hit
body: Johnny Blaze came back in 1992, the two Riders got a second title in Spirits of Vengeance, and Marvel then did what Marvel did in 1992: turned a successful book into an imprint. Rise of the Midnight Sons is a six-part crossover that launches Morbius, Nightstalkers and Darkhold off the back of Ghost Rider's sales, and for two years the titles run as one interlocking horror line — Midnight Massacre in 1993, then Siege of Darkness, seventeen chapters across every book at once, in 1994.

This is the most 1993 material on the site and it should be read as such: foil covers, bagged polybags, crossovers as a distribution strategy. It is also genuinely the high point of the character's commercial life, and Adam Kubert's Spirits of Vengeance is the run that made his name.
The line did not survive the crash. By 1995 the Midnight Sons books were gone; Ghost Rider itself limped to #93 in 1998 and then the character had no title at all for three years.

fig.cap: Left: Spirits of Vengeance #1 — Adam Kubert. Right: Morbius #1, launched out of the same crossover.

makers.b: Look at how he breaks the panel border. Kubert was working out the aggressive, tilted, overlapping page he would take to Wolverine and X-Men, and you can watch it being assembled here.

sections.h: 2099, and a Ghost Rider made of software
body: Marvel's 2099 line took each flagship character and asked what the name would mean in a corporate cyberpunk future. Ghost Rider 2099 is the one that answers best, because the premise transfers exactly: Zero Cochrane is a hacker murdered by a corporation, his mind dumped to the net by three artificial ghosts, and rebuilt inside a warbot with a flaming skull for a head. Vengeance, a machine, a bargain with something you do not control.

Len Kaminski writes it straight — no winking — in the register of Neuromancer, five years before The Matrix. And the early issues are drawn by Chris Bachalo before he became Chris Bachalo: tighter and more conventional than his later work, but already cramming a page with machinery.
Twenty-five issues, cancelled with the rest of the 2099 line, complete on this shelf.

fig.cap: Left: #1, 1994 — Bachalo. Right: #13, by which point the line had gone properly strange.

sections.h: Nine years of not knowing what to do with him
body: Nothing from this stretch has an omnibus and there is a reason: nothing from it lasted. Devin Grayson and Trent Kaniuga's 2001 Marvel Knights series is six issues. Garth Ennis and Clayton Crain's Road to Damnation in 2005 is six more, and is the best-regarded thing the character did in twenty years — Ennis writing it as a grubby, funny, extremely violent Western, and Crain painting it digitally in a way nothing else on the stands looked like.

Then the 2007 Nicolas Cage film, and a new ongoing to catch the traffic. Daniel Way wrote its first nineteen issues. Those nineteen issues are also not collected in omnibus, which is why the Aaron volume on this shelf opens at #20 rather than #1.

fig.cap: Left: Devin Grayson's 2001 Marvel Knights series. Right: Ennis and Crain, 2005 — neither is on the shelf.

sections.h: Jason Aaron decides it was never the devil
body: Jason Aaron takes over at #20 and immediately does the one thing thirty-five years of Ghost Rider comics had not: he changes where the curse comes from. The Ghost Riders were not made in hell. They were made in heaven, as weapons, and the angel who made them — Zadkiel — is now trying to storm the gates and needs them out of the way.

That single move turns a haunted-man book into a road movie with a war in it: a lineage of Riders going back centuries, a chain-smoking Caretaker, and Sister Sara, a nun with a shotgun and a motorcycle. Aaron was writing Scalped at the same time and the crime-fiction pacing carries straight over.
Roland Boschi and Tan Eng Huat do most of the drawing, and the run ends properly — Heaven's on Fire is a real finale, which is rare on this shelf.

fig.cap: Left: #20 — where the volume starts and Aaron starts. Right: #28, Tan Eng Huat.

makers.b: Notice how often a scene is two people talking in a diner or on a roadside before anything catches fire. Aaron writes supernatural horror on a crime-fiction chassis, and the dialogue is doing the work the splash pages get credit for.

sections.h: Robbie Reyes, and the other hole in the shelf
body: All-New Ghost Rider (2014) gives the name to Robbie Reyes, an East Los Angeles teenager looking after a disabled younger brother, and swaps the motorcycle for a possessed 1969 Dodge Charger. Felipe Smith wrote it and Tradd Moore drew it, and Moore's work on it is the most distinctive art any Ghost Rider book has had since Ploog: rubbery, elongated, every figure in motion, closer to skate graphics than to Marvel house style.
It has no omnibus. Neither does the 2016 or 2019 series. So the shelf jumps from 2010 straight to a book about somebody else entirely.

fig.cap: Tradd Moore's #1, 2014. Not on this shelf, and the clearest single omission on it after the 1972 run.

sections.h: The Punisher, a thousand years later, on fire
body: Donny Cates and Geoff Shaw invented the Cosmic Ghost Rider inside somebody else's comic. Thanos #13–18 — “Thanos Wins” — sends Thanos to a dead future to meet his older self, and the herald waiting there is Frank Castle: he made a deal with Mephisto, then a deal with Galactus, and has spent a millennium as a chain-swinging idiot on a burning space bike.

The joke is the whole character, and what Cates then does is refuse to stop telling it — five issues in which Frank tries to fix the universe by kidnapping the infant Thanos and raising him properly, which is very funny and then abruptly is not.
It is the least Ghost Rider thing on the shelf: no curse, no penance, no haunting. It is a cosmic comedy, and it works on its own terms.

fig.cap: Left: Thanos #13, where he is invented. Right: his own #1, a year later.

sections.h: Percy writes it as the horror novel it always was
body: Benjamin Percy is a horror novelist first — The Dark Net, The Ninth Metal — and Marvel handed him the fiftieth-anniversary relaunch in February 2022. He opens it with Johnny Blaze in Hayden Falls: a wife, two children, an auto shop, a small town in permanent late summer, and no memory of ever having been on fire.

The book spends its first arc letting you work out what that place is, and the register is openly Blue Velvet rather than superhero comics. Cory Smith draws the ordinary scenes with the same density as the supernatural ones, which is what makes the town feel wrong before anything has happened.
It runs to #21, crosses over with Percy's own Wolverine, and finishes in Final Vengeance in 2024 — the last Ghost Rider story before the title went away again, and currently the end of this shelf.

makers.b: Watch the first three pages of any issue. Percy opens on something domestic and slightly off — a diner, a hospital corridor, a family kitchen — and lets it curdle. He is building dread on a schedule, which is a novelist's habit and very unusual in a licensed monthly.

tone.sub: Seven books, and at least five different opinions about what a Ghost Rider comic is for.

modes.b: The three Danny Ketch volumes, and Vol. 2 especially. Texeira's black ink, an entire horror imprint launched off one title's sales, and a seventeen-part crossover. Start here if you want the version that sold.
Percy's run. A small town that is wrong, dread built on a schedule, and a novelist's pacing. The only book here that is frightening rather than loud.
Jason Aaron. Reassigns the curse from hell to heaven, invents a lineage of Riders going back centuries, and actually finishes what it started.
Ghost Rider 2099. Straight-faced cyberpunk with a warbot in the lead, written five years before The Matrix and drawn by early Chris Bachalo. A different man, a different genre, complete in 25 issues.
Cosmic Ghost Rider. The Punisher a thousand years on, doing bits. No curse, no penance, no haunting — and two-thirds of the volume is other people's comics.

dk-o1.title: Ghost Rider: Danny Ketch Omnibus Vol. 1
dk-o1.lede: A new man in the head, the Penance Stare, and Mark Texeira inventing the way the whole decade would look.

sections.h: A teenager who is not driving
body: Danny Ketch is hiding in a Cypress Hills scrapyard with his sister bleeding out when he touches the gas cap of a wrecked motorcycle. What stands up afterwards is not him.

That is the run's whole engine. The Rider is a separate person — it talks, it judges, it does not take instruction, and it regards Danny as transport. Where the 1972 book was a man cursed with a monster, this is a man sharing a body with a stranger who is better at everything, and Howard Mackie plays it for years without resolving it.

The Penance Stare is introduced here and is the most durable idea anyone has had about the character: meet its eyes and you experience every pain you have ever inflicted, simultaneously. It is a punishment rather than an attack, and it only works on the guilty — which quietly makes the Rider a judge.

The volume is not only the ongoing. It carries the Hearts of Darkness one-shot with Wolverine and the Punisher, and fifty-five issues' worth of Marvel Comics Presents backups, which are eight pages at a time and are where a lot of the era's guest artists turn up.

makers.b: Put an early Saltares-only page beside a Texeira one. The drawing underneath barely changes; what changes is that half the page becomes solid black and the flame is left as untouched white. Texeira is lighting the book rather than rendering it, and every Ghost Rider artist since has had to decide whether to copy him.
The bike. Saltares draws the machine with real weight and correct proportions, which sounds trivial and is not — it is the thing that keeps a flaming skull from floating.

fig.cap: Left: #1, 1990. Right: Hearts of Darkness, the one-shot that put him in a room with Wolverine and the Punisher.

body: This is the version of Ghost Rider that sold in enormous numbers, and the affection for it is real and largely nostalgic — readers who were fourteen in 1990 rate it very highly indeed.

The recurring criticism is that Mackie's plotting is thin under the art: villains arrive, get stared at, and are gone, and the mystery of who the Rider actually is gets stretched a long way. Nobody argues about Texeira.
It is also the easiest entry point on the shelf, because it is a genuine #1 and assumes you know nothing.

dk-o2.title: Ghost Rider: Danny Ketch Omnibus Vol. 2
dk-o2.lede: Johnny Blaze comes back, the two Riders get a second title, and Marvel builds an entire horror imprint on the back of one hit.

sections.h: Rise of the Midnight Sons
body: The crossover this volume is built around is a piece of publishing as much as a story: six chapters that launch three new ongoing titles at once. Ghost Rider #28, Spirits of Vengeance #1, Morbius #1, Nightstalkers #1, Darkhold #1, Ghost Rider #31 — and the book prints them in that reading order, which is why the contents jump from #28 to #31 and back.

What it buys, read now, is a snapshot of a Marvel that briefly had a functioning horror line: Morbius, Blade, Hannibal King, the Darkhold Redeemers and Lilith, Mother of Demons, all interlocking. Very little of it has aged into respectability and quite a lot of it is fun.

Adam Kubert draws Spirits of Vengeance, which pairs Danny with Johnny Blaze — back after nine years, older, angrier and carrying a shotgun that fires hellfire. The two-Riders dynamic is the best thing Mackie does in the whole decade.

makers.b: Watch the panel borders. Kubert tilts them, overlaps them and lets figures burst through, and the page reads as unstable on purpose. He takes this straight to Wolverine and it becomes one of the defining looks of the decade.

fig.cap: Left: Spirits of Vengeance #1. Right: Ghost Rider #31, the last chapter of Rise of the Midnight Sons.

sections.h: Midnight Massacre, and why the chapter list looks like that
body: The volume's second crossover runs Ghost Rider #40, Darkhold #11, Morbius #12 and Spirits of Vengeance #13 as a single story, and again the book prints it in reading order rather than in numerical order.

So the chapter list on this page has twenty-two chapters for fifty-five issues, several of them a single issue long. That is the book, not a chaptering error: naming Nightstalkers #1 as its own chapter tells you which comic you are in, where “Part 4” would not.

The Midnight Sons era is the character's commercial high point and its critical low, and both are true at once. This is crossover-driven publishing at the height of the speculator boom, with all the padding that implies.

Its defenders point out, fairly, that the interlocking horror line is a thing Marvel has never successfully done again, and that Adam Kubert's art here is genuinely important. Its detractors find it a marketing document with comics attached.
The Johnny Blaze material is the part most people agree on. Two Ghost Riders who do not like each other is a better book than one.

dk-o3.title: Ghost Rider: Danny Ketch Omnibus Vol. 3
dk-o3.lede: Siege of Darkness, Ron Garney's arrival, and the double-length #50 — the last good year before the line collapsed.

sections.h: Ships October 2026
body: This volume has not shipped yet. It is on the shelf ahead of that date because the three things a tile is made of are all real for it: the wiki carries its full contents, its issues resolve to marvel.com, and a jacket exists. Its badge retires itself in October without an edit.

One thing about that jacket is worth saying, because it looks like a mistake and is not: it carries no omnibus trade dress at all — no Marvel corner box, no creator credit block, just Henry Martinez's cover art and the 1990s logo. Marvel's own retail listing shows the same thing. That is the book.

sections.h: Siege of Darkness
body: Seventeen chapters across every Midnight Sons title at once, and the volume prints the Ghost Rider half of it interleaved exactly as it was read — which is why this page has twenty-eight chapters and most of them are one issue long.
It is the last time the line worked. Within a year Nightstalkers, Darkhold and Morbius were all cancelled, and Ghost Rider itself had four years left.

Ron Garney takes over the pencils in this stretch and is the best storyteller the book had after Texeira — cleaner, more legible, more interested in where a figure is standing. He goes on to Captain America with Mark Waid two years later.

Ghost Rider #50 is the double-length anniversary issue, with five artists on it including Garney and Adam Kubert. Note the wiki lists it twice, because it holds two separate stories — the shelf counts it once.

The tail of the volume is the oddest material here: Blaze: Legacy of Blood, a four-issue prestige mini, and the single issue of Ghost Rider and the Midnight Sons Magazine. Neither is on Marvel Unlimited, and both show a grey Read button on this shelf.

makers.b: Compare a Garney fight to a Texeira one. Texeira gives you an image; Garney gives you a sequence you can follow — where everyone is standing, which way they are facing, what happened between panel two and panel three. It is a less fashionable skill and a rarer one.

fig.cap: Left: Ghost Rider #44, Siege of Darkness. Right: Nightstalkers #14 — the same crossover, another book.

verdict.standing: The best of the Mackie run
body: Readers who rate the 1990s Ghost Rider highly usually mean this stretch — Garney's art, the Blaze/Ketch double act at full strength, and a crossover with an actual ending.

The reservation is the same one the whole era attracts: Siege of Darkness is seventeen parts, and this book gives you the Ghost Rider slice of it, so a few chapters read like the middle of a conversation. The volume note tells you which ones.
Unshipped as of now, so nobody has read it in this form. What it collects is well established.

gr2099-o1.title: Ghost Rider 2099 Omnibus
gr2099-o1.lede: A murdered hacker downloaded into a warbot. Straight-faced cyberpunk, complete in twenty-five issues, and drawn by Chris Bachalo before anyone knew who that was.

sections.h: The premise transfers exactly
body: Most of Marvel's 2099 line worked by putting a costume on a future. This one works because the underlying idea survives the translation: Zero Cochrane is killed by corporate security, his mind is pulled out of his dying body by three artificial intelligences calling themselves the Ghostworks, and he wakes up inside a cybernetic warbot he does not control and cannot leave.

A bargain with a power you do not understand, a body that is not yours, and vengeance as the only thing on the agenda. It is a Ghost Rider comic with every supernatural element replaced by a technological one, and nothing is lost.
Len Kaminski plays it entirely straight, in the register of Neuromancer — corporate arcologies, black ICE, a data-haven underclass — five years before The Matrix made that visual language mainstream.

Chris Bachalo draws the opening stretch. This is early Bachalo: much more conventional than the compressed, ornamental pages he is known for now, but already unusually dense, and already interested in machinery for its own sake. Kyle Hotz and Ashley Wood follow.
Twenty-five issues, cancelled with the rest of the line, and complete here — which is more than most books on this shelf can say.

makers.b: Look at the backgrounds rather than the figures. Bachalo fills the depth of every panel with hardware, and the density is the world-building — the script never has to explain that this future is cluttered and industrial, because the art has already said so.

fig.cap: Left: #1, 1994. Right: #13 — by which point the 2099 line had put him in charge of what was left of America.

body: Nearly forgotten for twenty-five years and then increasingly well spoken of, for the usual cult reasons: it is short, it is complete, it commits to its premise, and it looks like nothing else with the name on it.

The honest reservation is that it is not Johnny Blaze or Danny Ketch, and a reader who wants the Spirit of Vengeance rather than a cyberpunk novel will find that it shares a logo and very little else. It is on this shelf for the same reason Maestro is on the Hulk shelf.
The art falls off after Bachalo leaves, which is the most common specific complaint.

aaron-o1.title: Ghost Rider by Jason Aaron Omnibus
aaron-o1.lede: The curse comes from heaven, not hell — and the book becomes a road movie with a nun, a shotgun and a war in the sky.

sections.h: Reassigning the contract
body: For thirty-five years the Ghost Rider was a deal with the devil. Jason Aaron takes the book at #20 and says it never was: the Riders were forged in heaven as instruments of divine punishment, and Zadkiel — an angel planning a coup against the throne — wants them off the board before he moves.

It is a genuinely good retcon, because it makes the Penance Stare make sense. A punishment that only works on the guilty is a judicial instrument, not a demonic one, and Aaron simply follows the logic that was already there.

What it unlocks is scale. There is not one Ghost Rider, there are centuries of them — a lineage, a caretaker, an archive, and a lot of very strange people on motorcycles. Sister Sara, a nun with a shotgun, is the best character the book has had since Blaze.
Aaron was writing Scalped at Vertigo at the same time, and it shows in the pacing: long conversational scenes on roadsides and in diners, then sudden and very ugly violence.
Note where the volume starts. Daniel Way wrote #1–19 and that run has no omnibus, so the book opens at #20 with Aaron. It ends on Heaven's on Fire, which is a real ending — rare here.

makers.b: The grime. Boschi draws texture into everything — road surface, denim, skin — so the supernatural material lands in a world that already looks used. It is the opposite of Texeira's high-contrast approach and it suits Aaron's dialogue better.

Faces. Tan pushes anatomy well past realism — long jaws, hunched shoulders, everyone slightly wrong — and the effect is that the human characters look nearly as unnatural as the burning one. On a book about people who have been used by heaven, that is the point.

fig.cap: Left: #20, where Aaron starts. Right: Heaven's on Fire — the finale.

body: Widely held to be the best sustained run the character has had, and the one most often recommended to a reader who has never picked up a Ghost Rider comic. Aaron went on to Thor, Southern Bastards and a five-year Avengers run, and this is where a lot of people first noticed him.

Two fair criticisms. The heaven retcon annoys long-time readers who liked the deal-with-the-devil simplicity, and the mythology gets baroque in the back half — by Heaven's on Fire there are a great many Riders on the page.
The volume also has the shelf's most awkward starting point, at #20 of a series whose first nineteen issues are not collected here.

cosmic-o1.title: Cosmic Ghost Rider Omnibus
cosmic-o1.lede: Frank Castle, a thousand years dead, on a burning space bike — and two-thirds of this book is other people's comics.

sections.h: Invented inside a Thanos comic
body: Donny Cates and Geoff Shaw did not set out to make a Ghost Rider book. Thanos #13–18 — “Thanos Wins” — drops the present-day Thanos into a burnt-out future to meet the version of himself who won, and the herald who comes to collect him is the Punisher: dead, damned, cosmically powered and extremely pleased about it.
The character was a throwaway and became the most popular thing in the story, which is why the omnibus opens with six issues of a Thanos comic. The volume is honest about what it is.

Geoff Shaw's design work is a large part of why it landed: the skull is wrong in the right ways, the bike is a piece of Kirby machinery, and the whole figure reads as a joke and a threat in the same silhouette.

fig.cap: Left: Thanos #13, where he is invented. Right: his own #1.

sections.h: The joke, told until it stops being one
body: The five-issue solo series is about Frank deciding to fix the universe by going back in time and raising the infant Thanos properly. It is played broad, with Dylan Burnett drawing it in a loose cartoon line that is the correct call, and then in the last act it turns and asks what a man who has spent a thousand years killing actually thinks he is for.

Around it: Cosmic Ghost Rider Destroys Marvel History, which is exactly what it says and is a comedy book, Revenge of the Cosmic Ghost Rider by Christos Gage, and appearances in Guardians of the Galaxy and Avengers.
Seventeen of the thirty-five issues here are not his book. That is the trade this volume asks you to make, and it is the reason it sits at the odd end of this shelf.

verdict.standing: Very funny, barely a Ghost Rider book
body: Thanos Wins is the part everyone rates, and it is genuinely one of the best-regarded cosmic Marvel stories of the last decade. The Cosmic Ghost Rider material that follows is fondly held but is understood as a comedy spin-off, and the reception thins out across the later minis.

The recurring complaint about the omnibus specifically is composition: a reader who buys a Ghost Rider omnibus and gets six issues of Thanos, six of Guardians and four of Avengers has a point, even though every one of them is needed to follow the character.
If you want the Spirit of Vengeance, this is not it and does not pretend to be. If you want a very good bad idea executed with total commitment, it is the best thing on the shelf.

percy-o1.title: Ghost Rider by Benjamin Percy Omnibus
percy-o1.lede: A horror novelist gets the fiftieth-anniversary relaunch and opens it with Johnny Blaze in a small town that does not exist.

sections.h: Ships October 2026
body: This volume has not shipped yet and is on the shelf ahead of that for the same reason Vol. 3 of the Danny Ketch run is: contents, links and jacket are all real. Its badge retires itself in October.

Its cover here is a small flat scan taken from a bookseller rather than the wiki's file, because the wiki's image is the cover art without the trade dress — no logo, no credit block. It will be replaced with a proper scan when the book lands.

sections.h: Hayden Falls
body: Johnny Blaze has a wife, two children, an auto shop and a small town in permanent late summer. He does not remember being on fire. The first arc is about the reader working out what that place is before he does, and the reference point is openly Blue Velvet rather than anything from Marvel.

Benjamin Percy is a horror novelist — The Dark Net, The Ninth Metal — and he is one of very few writers to bring the actual machinery of the genre to a licensed monthly: withheld information, a slow curdle, and dread built to a schedule.

The back half goes wider. Percy was writing Wolverine and X-Force at the same time, which is where Weapons of Vengeance comes from, and the run closes in Final Vengeance in 2024 — the last Ghost Rider story before the title went away, and currently the end of this shelf.

The chapter list here alternates between the ongoing and one-shots because that is how the book prints them: Vengeance Forever, the annual and the two crossover bookends sit inside the run, not after it.

makers.b: Look at how he draws the ordinary scenes. Smith renders a kitchen or a garage with exactly the same density and shadow weight as a demon, so Hayden Falls feels wrong before anything supernatural has happened. Most artists save the heavy rendering for the monster; the whole trick here is not doing that.

body: Well received, and specifically praised for treating the book as horror rather than as an action title with a skull in it — which readers note is rarer than it should be for this character.

The criticisms are structural rather than about quality: the run gets pulled into line-wide crossover work in its second half, and readers who loved the contained small-town opening find the later Wolverine material a different book. Final Vengeance is generally thought a strong ending.
Unshipped as of now, so the omnibus itself is unreviewed. The comics in it are not.
